opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I get a lot, and my honest answer is that we're closer than most people thought five years ago, but further than the demo videos might suggest.

What changed is that robotics finally got a good recipe for generalization. For decades every robot was programmed for one task in one environment. If you moved the table ten centimeters, things broke. Now, with large foundation models, especially vision-language-action models built on top of models trained on internet-scale data, robots can understand open-ended instructions, recognize objects they've never seen in training, and transfer some common sense into physical actions. That's a qualitative shift. A robot can now be told, "put the snack that's healthy into the bowl," and it can figure out which object that is and roughly how to do it.

But being useful in everyday life is a much higher bar than doing something impressive in a lab. I think about three gaps.

The first is reliability. A demo succeeding seven or eight times out of ten is exciting for researchers, but in someone's home you need something like 99.9 percent, because every failure means a broken cup or a frustrated person. Getting from 80 to 99 percent is often harder than getting from 0 to 80.

The second is dexterity and the long tail of physical interaction. Language and vision benefited from huge amounts of internet data. For physical actions, contact, force, how a towel deforms, how much pressure to use on a tomato, there's no equivalent dataset. We're trying to close that with simulation, with large-scale teleoperation, with learning from human videos, but data is still the main bottleneck.

The third is cost and safety. A general-purpose robot has to be affordable and safe enough to operate next to children, pets, and elderly people. Hardware is getting cheaper fast, partly thanks to the humanoid and quadruped push, but we're not at consumer-appliance pricing yet.

So my prediction is that it won't be a single moment where the robot butler shows up. It'll be gradual. First in semi-structured settings like warehouses, factories, logistics, and retail back rooms, where tasks are varied but the environment is somewhat controlled. Then in places like hospitals and elder care for specific assistive tasks. Homes will be the last and hardest frontier. I'd say within a few years we'll see general-purpose robots doing genuinely useful work commercially, and over roughly the next decade they'll start to enter homes in meaningful numbers.

What makes me optimistic is that, for the first time, progress feels like it's on a scaling curve. More data, better models, and better hardware compound on each other. In my career that's never been true for robotics before, and it's why I think this time really is different.

r001.rationale: It contrasts historically task-specific robots with newer generalization and says home use remains difficult, but does not clearly state that current robots are proficient at narrowly defined tasks while broad task competence remains distant.

r002.rationale: It identifies dexterity and physical interaction as challenges, but does not compare fine manipulation reliability with simple pick-and-place.

r003.rationale: It says demo performance of 7–8 successes out of 10 is inadequate for home use, where it estimates 99.9% reliability is needed; this clearly makes a 30–40% success rate insufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think we're closer than most people expect, but further than the demo videos suggest. Both things are true at once.

Let me explain what I mean. On the research side, the last two or three years have been a genuine shift. We used to build a robot for one task, in one environment, with a lot of hand-engineering. Now, with foundation models, we're training a single policy that can take a language instruction, look at a scene it has never seen before, and do something reasonable. That used to feel like science fiction. When I started in this field, the idea that you could just tell a robot "put the cup in the sink" and have it work in a new kitchen was a research dream. Now it works some fraction of the time, and that fraction keeps going up.

But there's a huge gap between "works some fraction of the time" and "useful in your home." If a robot does the dishes correctly ninety percent of the time, you still can't trust it, because the ten percent is when it drops your grandmother's plate. Everyday life is unforgiving. You need reliability, you need safety around people and pets, and you need it to recover gracefully when something goes wrong. That last mile is hard, and I think it's where most of the remaining work is.

The other bottleneck is data. Language models had the whole internet. Robots don't have that. Every physical interaction has to be collected either through teleoperation, which is expensive, or through simulation, which is where a lot of my own work has been. I'm fairly optimistic about simulation plus real-world fine-tuning as a path, but the sim-to-real gap is still something you fight every single day.

So if you ask me for a timeline, I'd say structured environments first. Warehouses, factories, hospitals, maybe hotels. Those are already starting to happen because the environment is semi-controlled and the economics are clear. For a general-purpose robot that's actually helpful in a messy home, I think we're talking about several years for the first real products, and probably a decade before it feels normal. But I would have said twenty years if you'd asked me three years ago, so the slope matters more than the number.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts robots built for one task in one environment with newer policies that handle language instructions and unfamiliar scenes, then says useful home robots remain years away.

r002.rationale: It discusses household reliability and dropped dishes but does not compare fine manipulation with simple pick-and-place tasks.

r003.rationale: It says even 90% success may be too unreliable, but does not state or assess a 30–40% success rate.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we mean by useful. A robot that helps with a few specific tasks in a fairly predictable environment is much closer than a robot that can walk into any home and do whatever you ask.

The challenge is reliability. Doing something successfully once is very different from doing it every day, with different objects, different layouts, and people moving around. In a home, a robot also has to recognize when it doesn’t know what to do and stop safely or ask for help.

So I expect progress to be gradual. We’ll see robots become useful for a limited set of tasks, and then those capabilities will expand. I’m optimistic, but I would be cautious about giving a precise date for a truly general-purpose household robot.

r001.rationale: It says robots are closer to helping with a few specific tasks in predictable settings than to handling any request in any home.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability generally but does not compare fine manipulation with simple pick-and-place tasks.

r003.rationale: It gives no 30–40 percent success rate or judgment that such a rate is insufficient for everyday use.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re getting closer, but there’s still a big gap between an impressive demonstration and a robot that you’d want in your home. In a demo, a robot might succeed once. In everyday life, it needs to succeed reliably, handle unexpected situations, and be safe around people.

The hard part is that our homes are so varied. Picking up a cup sounds simple, but the cup could be transparent, slippery, half full, or hidden behind something else. And if the robot makes a mistake, it needs to recognize that and recover.

So I expect progress to come in stages. We’ll see robots become useful for particular tasks in more controlled environments first. Those capabilities will gradually expand. I’m optimistic about general-purpose robots, but I’d be cautious about putting a precise date on when one can do most of your household chores.

r001.rationale: It says robots will first become useful for particular tasks in controlled environments, while broader household capability will expand gradually.

r002.rationale: It describes challenges with picking up a cup, but does not compare fine manipulation reliability with simple pick-and-place tasks.

r003.rationale: It does not mention a 30–40 percent success rate or judge that rate insufficient for everyday use.
